What if a giant asteroid slammed into the Moon?
Earth has an atmosphere that burns rocks up. The Moon has nothing. So this one arrives at full speed: tens of thousands of kilometres per hour.
Imagine a rock one kilometre wide. In an instant, it hits.
It carves a crater over ten kilometres across, and the rock itself melts and vaporizes.
But here's the eerie part: no sound. No air means no boom, no mushroom cloud. Just silent debris flying in perfect arcs.
From Earth, you'd see a flash. We've actually seen this: in 2013, a small meteoroid lit up the Moon so brightly that telescopes caught it.
Some debris could even reach us. In fact, pieces of the Moon have already landed on Earth as meteorites.
Would it knock the Moon off course, or change our tides? No. The Moon is far too massive.
Ancient impacts were far bigger. One carved a basin two thousand five hundred kilometres wide, and the Moon itself was likely born from a giant collision.
So next time you look up, remember: that's a world covered in scars. Follow for more what-ifs.
